chunks: Ibn Maḥbūb narrated from ʿAlī ibn Riʾāb, from Zurārah, who said:

I asked Abā Jaʿfar عليه السلام about a man who was killed, and he had a brother in the abode of migration, and a brother in the abode of the Bedouin, and he had not migrated. What do you say: if the Emigrant pardons, but the Bedouin wants to kill, does he have that right?
He said: He عليه السلام said: “The Bedouin does not have the right to kill an Emigrant until he migrates.” He said: “So when the Emigrant pardons, then his pardon is valid.”
I said: Does the Bedouin have any share of the inheritance? He عليه السلام said: “As for inheritance, he has his allotted share from the blood-money of his brother, if it is taken.”

key_terms.الْبَدَوِيُّ: the Bedouin heir who has not migrated
key_terms.الْمُهَاجِرُ: the migrant heir whose legal pardon is recognized here
key_terms.دَارِ الْبَدْوِ: the abode of the Bedouin; the desert dwelling of the nomadic Arabs
key_terms.دَارِ الْهِجْرَةِ: the abode of migration; the land associated with those who migrated
key_terms.دِيَةِ: blood-money paid in compensation for unlawful killing
key_terms.عَفَا: pardoned or waived the claim of retaliation

ai.seo_question: Does a non-migrant Bedouin heir have the right to demand retaliation if a migrant heir pardons the killer?
ai.summary: This hadith discusses a legal ruling concerning the differing rights of heirs in a retaliation case when one brother is a muhājir and the other is a Bedouin who has not migrated. It states that the non-migrant Bedouin does not have the authority to carry out retaliation in this case, while the pardon of the migrant heir is valid, and the Bedouin still retains his share from the diyah if it is taken.
